justice: The roadway allocates substantial space to motor vehicles with multiple wide lanes, while the pedestrian sidewalk on the right is comparatively narrow, indicating an uneven distribution of street space among users.
A dedicated side lane used by cyclists or low-speed two-wheelers is visibly separated from the main carriageway by solid lane markings, which improves spatial provision for non-motorized users.

The right-side sidewalk appears continuous and level, but no curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked pedestrian crossings are visible in the scene, limiting evidence of fully inclusive access for all users.
safety: The central planted median separates opposing traffic flows, reducing the likelihood of head-on conflicts on this wide arterial road.
Cyclists and electric two-wheelers travel in a designated side lane rather than mixing directly with fast-moving cars in the main lanes, which improves safety for both cyclists and drivers.

Clear white lane markings and a relatively orderly road geometry support legibility and predictable movement, but the apparent high design speed of the corridor still creates risk for slower users near the curbside lane.
livability: The corridor is dominated by fast-moving traffic infrastructure and long travel lanes, with little visible street-level activity, storefronts, or social destinations that would support everyday public life.
A sidewalk exists on the right side, but there are no visible benches, kiosks, bus shelters, or gathering spaces that would make the street edge more usable for lingering or social interaction.
The dense tree line and landscaped median add some environmental quality, yet the overall setting reads more as a through-traffic boulevard than a lively neighborhood street.
sustainability: The presence of a dedicated side lane accommodating bicycles or electric two-wheelers supports lower-carbon travel options beyond private car use.
The planted median and continuous tree belt on the right provide substantial greenery, which contributes to urban ecological value and some heat-mitigation benefits.
Despite the green elements, the very wide multi-lane carriageway still prioritizes automobile throughput, which limits the overall sustainability performance of the corridor.
aesthetics: The long rows of trees on the right and the planted central median create a green, visually coherent landscape along the corridor.
Streetlights are regularly spaced and the road surface appears clean and well maintained, giving the avenue an orderly and polished appearance.

The open sky view and consistent boulevard geometry create a strong sense of visual spaciousness, although the scene is somewhat monotonous due to limited architectural detail and human-scale elements.
comfort: The broad tree belt along the right side likely improves thermal comfort near the sidewalk and edge lane, even though direct shade over the pavement is limited in the visible section.
The asphalt surfaces for both the main road and side lane appear smooth and even, supporting physical comfort for drivers and cyclists.
Psychological comfort is mixed: the corridor feels uncluttered and spacious, but the width of the roadway and fast-traffic character can feel inhospitable for pedestrians on the narrow edge sidewalk.
walkability: A continuous sidewalk is visible on the right, which provides a basic walking route separated from moving cars by the side lane and vegetation edge.
However, the street is an expansive arterial with no visible marked crosswalks, pedestrian signals, or curb extensions, making route connectivity and crossing convenience appear weak.
There are no visible benches, active frontages, or pedestrian-oriented amenities along the sidewalk, so walking is possible but not especially attractive or destination-rich.
bikeability: A dedicated curbside lane is clearly present and used by cyclists or electric two-wheelers, offering a more comfortable riding space than the main traffic lanes.
Solid lane markings separate this lane from adjacent motor traffic, reducing direct conflicts with faster vehicles and improving perceived safety.
The corridor appears long, straight, and smooth, which supports efficient cycling, but the lane is adjacent to a high-speed arterial and no physical barrier or bicycle parking is visible.
